questions.stem: What is bioinformatics?
options: Cutting and joining DNA molecules with restriction enzymes and ligase
Using computers to store and analyse data such as DNA sequences
Using bacteria to produce human proteins in large fermentation tanks
Selectively breeding organisms for useful traits over many generations
questions.explanation: Bioinformatics combines biology, computing and statistics to manage and analyse large data sets, such as genome sequences and protein structures. Cutting and joining DNA is genetic engineering.

questions.stem: Which is an example of genetic engineering?
options: Fermenting grape juice with yeast to produce wine
Grafting a branch from one apple tree onto another tree
Inserting a human gene into bacteria so that they make a human protein
Crossing two wheat varieties to combine their useful traits in one plant
questions.explanation: Genetic engineering directly alters an organism's DNA, for example by inserting a gene from another species. Crossing varieties is selective breeding, which works with existing alleles.

questions.stem: Which task in developing a gene therapy is an example of bioinformatics?
options: Inserting a working copy of the gene into a viral vector in the laboratory
Growing the modified virus in large numbers in cultured human cells
Injecting the finished gene therapy into the retina of a patient
Comparing a patient's DNA sequence with a database to locate a variant
questions.explanation: Searching sequence databases and analysing sequence data are bioinformatics tasks. Building the vector is genetic engineering, and giving the treatment is clinical medicine.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares transgenic organisms and genetically modified organisms (GMOs)?
options: Transgenic organisms are made by selective breeding, and GMOs by gene technology
GMOs contain DNA from another species, and transgenic organisms contain only their own
All transgenic organisms are GMOs, but a GMO need not contain DNA from another species
All GMOs are transgenic, but a transgenic organism need not have had its DNA altered
questions.explanation: A GMO is any organism whose genetic material has been altered by gene technology; it is transgenic only if the added DNA comes from a different species. So transgenic organisms are a subset of GMOs.

questions.stem: One plant is given an extra copy of one of its own genes by gene technology. A second plant receives a gene from a bacterium. How are they classified?
options: The first is a GMO but not transgenic; the second is transgenic
Both are transgenic, because both were made by genetic engineering
The first is transgenic; the second is a GMO but not transgenic
Neither is a GMO, because both genes came from living organisms
questions.explanation: Both plants have had their DNA altered by gene technology, so both are GMOs, but only the second contains DNA from another species, which makes it transgenic. The source of the gene being living is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Which comparison of germline changes made by reproductive and genetic engineering technologies is correct?
options: Both technologies change the DNA sequence of the embryo before it is implanted in the uterus
Neither technology affects the DNA that the resulting child could pass on to its descendants
IVF with embryo selection chooses among existing genomes; germline editing alters an embryo's DNA
IVF with embryo selection alters an embryo's DNA; germline editing chooses among existing genomes
questions.explanation: Embryo testing and selection picks embryos that do not carry a variant, so no DNA is changed, while germline gene editing changes an embryo's genome, and the change would be inherited. Both influence what the child can pass on.

questions.stem: Mitochondrial donation, made legal in Australia in 2022 under Maeve's Law, combines the parents' nuclear DNA with an egg from a donor with healthy mitochondria. Why is it a germline change?
options: It changes the DNA in the mother's body cells, which she then passes on to her children
The donor's nuclear DNA becomes part of the genome of every descendant of the child
The donor's mitochondrial DNA can be passed on through daughters to later generations
It edits the embryo's nuclear genes, and the edited genes are passed to descendants
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are inherited through the egg, so a girl born by this method can pass the donor's mitochondrial DNA to her own children. The nuclear DNA still comes from the two parents.

questions.stem: How does computer modelling of protein structure help in developing a biotechnology?
options: It replaces the need for clinical trials of any new drug made from the protein
It inserts the gene for the protein into the cells of the patient being treated
It predicts a protein's 3D shape, helping design drugs that bind it
It manufactures large amounts of the protein for use in medical treatments
questions.explanation: A protein's function depends on its shape, so models predicting structure from amino acid sequence help scientists design molecules that fit it. Models guide development but do not replace laboratory work and clinical trials.

questions.stem: Which biotechnology used in health was developed through Australian research?
options: Insulin, which was first extracted from the pancreas by scientists in Melbourne
The HPV vaccine, using virus-like particles developed in Queensland
The polio vaccine, which was first developed at the University of Sydney
Penicillin, which was first discovered at the CSIRO laboratories in Canberra
questions.explanation: Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou at the University of Queensland developed the virus-like particle technology used in HPV vaccines. Insulin was first isolated in Toronto, and the first polio vaccine was developed in the United States.

questions.stem: Australian newborns are screened for cystic fibrosis with a heel-prick blood test. If the first result is high, the same sample is tested for common CFTR variants. Which technology is used in this second step?
options: Measuring the glucose level in the baby's blood
DNA analysis, such as PCR, to detect specific variants
Karyotyping, to count the baby's chromosomes
Culturing bacteria from the baby's blood sample
questions.explanation: Variant testing amplifies and analyses the CFTR gene to see whether the baby carries known disease-causing alleles. A karyotype cannot detect a change of a few bases, and a positive result is usually confirmed with a sweat test.

questions.stem: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is diagnosed by measuring the protein in blood and by genotyping. Why is genotyping useful as well as measuring the protein level?
options: It shows whether the person has a lung infection that is lowering their protein level
It identifies which variant alleles the person carries, informing prognosis and family testing
It measures the amount of alpha-1 antitrypsin in the blood more accurately than a protein test
It cures the deficiency by correcting the variant allele in the person's liver cells
questions.explanation: Different variants cause different degrees of deficiency and risk, and knowing the genotype allows relatives to be tested for the same alleles. Genotyping identifies variants; it does not measure protein or treat the condition.

questions.stem: Inherited retinal dystrophies, such as Leber congenital amaurosis, can be caused by variants in any of more than 200 genes. Which approach is best suited to diagnosis?
options: Sequencing many genes or the whole exome and checking databases
Karyotyping the patient's cells to look for missing or extra chromosomes
A blood test for antibodies that the immune system makes against the retina
Testing a single gene chosen at random from those linked to the condition
questions.explanation: With so many possible genes, sequencing many at once and comparing the results with databases of known variants is the efficient route to a diagnosis. Point variants are invisible on a karyotype.

questions.stem: A couple planning a pregnancy have reproductive carrier screening for cystic fibrosis. What does this tell them?
options: The complete DNA sequence of the child they are planning to have
Whether each partner is a carrier, and so the risk to a child
Whether their future child will definitely be born with cystic fibrosis
Whether either partner currently shows any symptoms of cystic fibrosis
questions.explanation: Carriers are healthy, so screening reveals hidden variants; if both partners are carriers, each child has a 1 in 4 chance of cystic fibrosis. Screening the parents gives probabilities, not a certain outcome.

questions.stem: What is GenBank?
options: A store of frozen seeds from threatened plant species
A bank holding frozen sperm and eggs for IVF patients
A government database of patients' medical records
A public database of DNA sequences maintained by the NCBI
questions.explanation: GenBank, run by the US National Center for Biotechnology Information, holds publicly available nucleotide sequences submitted by researchers worldwide, and exchanges data with the EMBL database in Europe.

questions.stem: A researcher sequences the CFTR gene from a patient and searches GenBank using a tool such as BLAST. What does this allow?
options: Predicting the exact age at which the patient's symptoms will begin
Comparing the sequence with known sequences to identify any variants
Producing many more copies of the gene for further laboratory work
Inserting the gene into a plasmid so that bacteria can express it
questions.explanation: BLAST aligns a query sequence with sequences in the database, revealing differences from the reference and matches to known disease variants. Copying a gene is done by PCR, not by a database search.

questions.stem: Why might a genetic database underestimate how common a disease variant is in some populations?
options: The database contains the genome of every person living in each country
Disease-causing variants are removed from databases once they are found
Databases record only variants that are found in people with no disease
Groups under-represented in the database contribute few sequences to it
questions.explanation: Estimates of prevalence from a database reflect the people whose DNA is in it; if some ancestries are rarely sampled, their variants are missed or appear rare. Databases contain only a small sample of any population.

questions.stem: A woman learns from a genetic test that she carries a harmful BRCA1 variant. Which is a benefit of this information?
options: She now knows that she will definitely develop breast cancer
Her children are now certain to carry the same BRCA1 variant
The test has removed the harmful variant from her body cells
She can begin earlier screening or choose preventive surgery
questions.explanation: Knowing her higher risk lets her and her doctors act early, for example with more frequent imaging or risk-reducing surgery. The variant raises risk greatly but does not make cancer certain, and each child has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it.

questions.stem: Which is a risk of receiving personalised genetic information about the risk of a non-infectious disease?
options: The test permanently changes the DNA sequence in the person's body cells
The information cannot be kept, so it is lost soon after the test is done
The result always gives a certain diagnosis of whether the disease will occur
Anxiety, or false reassurance that leads to ignoring lifestyle risks
questions.explanation: Risk results can cause worry, and a low genetic score may lead someone to neglect diet, exercise or screening even though lifestyle strongly affects many diseases. Privacy and possible discrimination are further concerns.

questions.stem: What is somatic gene therapy?
options: Editing the DNA of an embryo so that the change passes to all future descendants
Treating a genetic condition with regular injections of the missing protein
Choosing an embryo without the faulty allele during IVF before implantation
Putting a working gene into body cells to treat a condition, not gametes
questions.explanation: Somatic gene therapy targets affected tissues such as the retina or blood stem cells, so it helps the patient but is not inherited. Editing embryos is germline modification, and protein injections are not gene therapy.

questions.stem: Luxturna treats Leber congenital amaurosis caused by variants in both copies of the RPE65 gene. A harmless viral vector carrying a working RPE65 gene is injected under the retina. What is the outcome?
options: Retinal cells make working RPE65 protein, and vision often improves
The faulty RPE65 alleles are removed from the patient's eggs or sperm
Every cell in the patient's body receives a working copy of the gene
The virus destroys the retinal cells that carry the faulty RPE65 alleles
questions.explanation: The vector delivers the gene only to retinal cells near the injection, which then make the missing protein needed for the visual cycle, improving light sensitivity in many patients. Gametes are unaffected, so children can still inherit the faulty allele.

questions.stem: Casgevy, a treatment for sickle cell disease, uses CRISPR-Cas9 to edit a patient's blood stem cells outside the body so they make fetal haemoglobin, then returns the cells. Why does this reduce the disease's effects?
options: It replaces the faulty beta-globin gene in every cell of the patient's body
It removes the sickle cell allele from the patient's eggs or sperm cells
It makes the patient's red blood cells divide faster than they are destroyed
Fetal haemoglobin does not sickle, so red cells work more normally
questions.explanation: Fetal haemoglobin uses gamma chains instead of beta chains, so it is unaffected by the sickle variant and dilutes the sickle haemoglobin in red cells. Only blood stem cells are edited, so the change is not inherited.

questions.stem: Which statement about the ethical and legal position of gene therapy in Australia is correct?
options: Somatic therapies can be approved, but heritable nuclear editing is banned
Editing embryos for a pregnancy is legal as long as both parents give informed consent
Gene therapies need no approval because they use the patient's own cells and genes
All forms of gene therapy are banned in Australia because they alter human DNA
questions.explanation: Somatic gene therapies are assessed for safety and effectiveness before approval, while making heritable changes to the nuclear genome of a human embryo is a criminal offence. Consent does not make a prohibited procedure legal.

questions.stem: Some gene therapies cost more than a million dollars per patient. Which ethical issue does this raise most directly?
options: Infection risk, because treated patients can pass the gene to others
Identity, because the therapy changes the patient's blood group
Consent, because gene therapy is given without the patient's knowledge
Equity of access, because not every patient or health system can pay
questions.explanation: Very high prices mean that access may depend on wealth or on public funding decisions, raising questions of fairness. Gene therapies are not contagious and are given with informed consent.

questions.stem: In producing recombinant insulin, why are the plasmid and the human insulin gene cut with the same restriction enzyme?
options: To translate the human gene into insulin inside the test tube
To give matching sticky ends that base-pair and can be joined by ligase
To remove the introns from the human gene before it is inserted
To make the plasmid carry a gene for resistance to antibiotics
questions.explanation: A restriction enzyme cuts at a specific sequence, so using the same enzyme gives complementary sticky ends on both pieces of DNA, which pair and are sealed by DNA ligase.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly models the production of recombinant human insulin?
options: Transform bacteria; obtain gene; join with ligase; cut gene and plasmid; purify; select and culture
Cut gene and plasmid; purify; transform bacteria; obtain gene; join with ligase; select and culture
Obtain gene; transform bacteria; cut gene and plasmid; purify; join with ligase; select and culture
Obtain gene; cut gene and plasmid; join with ligase; transform bacteria; select and culture; purify
questions.explanation: The gene must be obtained and joined into the plasmid before bacteria can take it up; transformed bacteria are then selected, grown in fermenters and the insulin purified. Purification is always the final step.

questions.stem: Why is the mRNA used to make the insulin gene extracted from pancreatic beta cells rather than from skin cells?
options: Beta cells contain bacterial plasmids that already carry the gene
Beta cells express the insulin gene, so are rich in its mRNA
Only beta cells contain the insulin gene in their nuclear DNA
Skin cells keep introns in their mRNA, but beta cells remove them
questions.explanation: Every body cell carries the insulin gene, but only beta cells transcribe it, so they are rich in insulin mRNA, which reverse transcriptase converts into intron-free DNA. Skin cells splice their mRNA too; they simply do not express insulin.

questions.stem: What is an advantage of recombinant human insulin over insulin extracted from pigs and cattle?
options: It matches human insulin and can be made in large, consistent amounts
It is made without using any living cells, which makes it cheaper and faster
It cures type 1 diabetes, so patients need only a single course of injections
It is taken as a tablet because bacteria change it so it survives digestion
questions.explanation: Bacteria or yeast carrying the human gene make insulin with the human amino acid sequence, avoiding supply limits and some reactions to animal insulin. It is made by living cells and still has to be injected.

questions.stem: In a trial, people with type 1 diabetes using a glucose sensor linked to an insulin pump spent on average 70% of the day in the target glucose range, compared with 55% for those injecting insulin. Which conclusion is most valid?
options: The pump system improved control on average, if the groups were randomised and similar
The pump system cures type 1 diabetes in most of the patients who start using it
Every patient using the pump had better control than every patient using injections
Injected insulin gives no benefit at all to people who have type 1 diabetes
questions.explanation: An average difference shows a benefit for the group, provided allocation was random so other factors were balanced; individuals vary, so some injecting patients may do better than some pump users. Both groups still have diabetes and need insulin.

questions.stem: CAR-T therapy is used for some blood cancers. What is the general approach?
options: T cells are removed, given a gene for a receptor that targets the cancer, multiplied and returned
Cancer cells are removed, edited to make them harmless, multiplied and returned to the patient
Antibodies from a donor who has recovered from cancer are injected into the patient
A vaccine of weakened cancer cells is injected so that the patient makes antibodies
questions.explanation: The patient's own T cells are genetically engineered to carry a chimeric antigen receptor that recognises a protein on the cancer cells, then grown in large numbers and infused, so they find and kill the cancer.

questions.stem: Which comparison of PCR testing and rapid antigen tests for a respiratory virus is correct?
options: Both tests detect the antibodies that the patient's immune system has made against the virus
PCR sequences the patient's whole genome, while antigen tests count the patient's white cells
PCR amplifies viral nucleic acid and is more sensitive; antigen tests detect viral proteins quickly
PCR detects viral proteins quickly; antigen tests amplify viral nucleic acid and are more sensitive
questions.explanation: PCR copies tiny amounts of viral genetic material many times, so it detects low levels of virus but needs a laboratory. Rapid antigen tests use antibodies on a strip to detect viral proteins within minutes, but miss more low-level infections.

questions.stem: Why is viral RNA converted to DNA with reverse transcriptase before PCR testing for an RNA virus such as influenza?
options: The polymerase used in PCR copies DNA, not RNA
RNA molecules are too large to fit in the PCR tube
Antibodies in the sample would destroy the RNA
Only DNA can be detected after it is amplified
questions.explanation: Taq polymerase uses a DNA template, so the RNA genome is first copied into complementary DNA, which is then amplified. This combined method is called reverse transcription PCR.

questions.stem: A blood test detects antibodies against a virus. Why is it less useful than PCR for diagnosing a new infection in its first few days?
options: Antibodies disappear completely as soon as an infection begins
Antibody tests detect the virus's RNA, which appears only later
Antibodies take days to weeks to appear after an infection begins
Antibodies are found only in people who have been vaccinated
questions.explanation: The primary adaptive response takes time, so antibodies may be undetectable early, while viral genetic material is present from the start. Antibody tests are more useful for showing past infection.

questions.stem: How does whole-genome sequencing of a pathogen taken from many patients help manage an outbreak?
options: It gives results faster than any rapid antigen test can be read
It measures how many antibodies each infected patient has made
It shows which cases are closely related, tracing spread and new variants
It cures patients by correcting the genes of the pathogen inside them
questions.explanation: Comparing pathogen genomes reveals chains of transmission, the source of an outbreak and the emergence of new variants, which guides control measures. Sequencing takes longer than a rapid test.

questions.stem: In the World Mosquito Program, Aedes aegypti mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria are released. How does this reduce dengue?
options: Wolbachia makes people immune to dengue after they are bitten by a mosquito
Wolbachia is a vaccine that the mosquitoes inject into people as they feed
Wolbachia limits virus replication in mosquitoes and spreads through them
Wolbachia kills every mosquito in the area within a few days of the release
questions.explanation: Mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia are much less able to transmit dengue, and the bacterium spreads through the local mosquito population, so transmission falls. It does not kill the mosquitoes or immunise people.

questions.stem: Why does Wolbachia spread through a wild mosquito population after release instead of dying out?
options: Released mosquitoes are larger, so they outcompete and kill all the wild mosquitoes
Infected females pass it to all offspring, and uninfected females mated by infected males lay eggs that do not hatch
Infected males pass it to all offspring, and infected females mated by uninfected males lay eggs that do not hatch
The bacterium is spread from mosquito to mosquito through the air, like a respiratory virus
questions.explanation: Wolbachia is inherited through the egg, and the incompatibility between infected males and uninfected females gives infected females a breeding advantage, so the bacterium's frequency rises each generation.

questions.stem: Male Aedes aegypti carrying a self-limiting gene that kills female offspring before adulthood are released. What is the expected result, and a limitation?
options: Fewer biting females over time, but releases must continue as the gene fades
All mosquito species in the area die out permanently after a single release
Females can no longer carry dengue, but the mosquito population keeps growing
The males begin biting people instead, so they spread the virus further
questions.explanation: Only female mosquitoes bite and transmit disease, so killing female offspring reduces the population, but the gene is lost after a few generations, so repeated releases are needed. Only the target species is affected.

questions.stem: Which is a potential societal benefit of using genetic technologies to manage infectious diseases?
options: Faster vaccine development, e.g. mRNA vaccines, in a pandemic
An end to the need for any public health measures in the future
The removal of every pathogen species from the environment
Permanent immunity to all diseases after a single treatment
questions.explanation: Genetic technologies such as rapid genome sequencing and mRNA vaccine platforms shorten the time from identifying a pathogen to having a vaccine, reducing illness, deaths and disruption. They support, rather than replace, other public health measures.
